translator: Claude (AI), draft, not reviewed by a Hittitologist
intro: This joined tablet (KBo 12.126 + KUB 24.9 + KBo 12.127 + a piece published in JCS 24) is the main manuscript of the ritual of Alli, woman of Arzawa, against bewitchment (CTH 402); her name is broken away in the first line here. The Old Woman sends the sorcery back to whoever cast it, using clay and wax figures, threads of five colours, the burial and nailing-down of the sorcery, offerings along the road, a night the patient spends sleeping over a basket of objects, purification with earth and dough, and offerings on a river bank. After the colophon comes a list of the ritual materials.

paras.en: […] woman of Arzawa: If a per[son] […] […] a [fig]ure of clay; among them two men(?), and a [kur]ša-bag (of leather) […] […] tongues are lying (there).

[…] clothed in kureššar-cloths(?); one kurtal-box(?) of clay, and it (is fitted) with a tongue of clay […] […] of [cl]ay, and it holds it lifted up; a shovel (intaluzzi-) (and) a rake (ḫaḫḫar-) of clay. […] And below each of them(?) she arranges three naktamu-vessels (lidded pots?) in the same way.

[…] the clay [fig]ure is smeared(?) all around on the outside, and all this she arranges in front of them. The person who is bewitched sits down facing the Sun-god, and the Old Woman takes the naktamu-vessel together with the clay figure and holds it up towards the Sun-god.

And the Old Woman speaks as follows: 'O Sun-god of the hand(?) (kiššeraš), see, (there are) sorcerous people! If a man has bewitched (lit. treated) this person, see, he (the patient) carries it lifted up on (his) back. Let him (the sorcerer) take it back for himself, and (then) he carries it lifted up on (his own) back.

[But i]f a [woma]n has bewitched him, you, Sun-god, know her. Let the kureššar-(headcloth) be hers, and let her keep it fastened on her head; [let] her take them back for herself! Let the išḫuzzi-(belt) be hers; let her gird herself with it! Let the shoes be hers; let her put them on!'

[…] the sorcery … […] let it be […], and let him take it (back) with (his) family(?). Let the [pi]g break loose from the peg and go back to its owner! […] She treats two naktamu-vessels in the same way.

[Then] the [Old] Woman says to the figures: 'Come(?)! What we have done(?), give it [ba]ck to us!' Thus (says) the human being: 'We can no longer hold out(?); we have become tired [under it(?)], and we have toiled with the illness(?). Take it back once more and carry it away!'

[The Sun-god] of the hand(?) and the dog-man (are) in front(?): he has his bow, [he has] his [arr]ows, and as for his dogs, he has four dogs. [For the ho]rses let there be imiul-fodder, and let there be clay figures of the person. [And] the [Old Wo]man sets [them] down.

The Old Woman places d[ark] wool of the knee(?) on the person, and the Old Woman [places it] up on his head [and] speaks [as follows]: 'Whoever has been [making] him d[ark](?), has been bewitching him — now, see, [I am tak]ing [the sorcery] from him and [giving] it back to his master.' She winds the thread (kapina-) around the figures.

[Afterw]ards she [makes] a thread of red wool in the same way [and speaks]: '[Whoev]er has been making him bloody, whoever has been bewi[tching] him — I am taking the [bloo]died sorcery and [gi]ving it [b]ack [to his master].' She winds the thread around the figures.

[Afterwar]ds she makes a thread of green wool in the same way and [speaks] as follows: '[Whoever] has bewitched this person, whoever has been making (him) pale (ḫaḫlaḫḫ-) — [now] I am taking the green sorcery from him and [giving] it back [to his mas]ter.' She winds the thread around the figures.

[Afterw]ards she makes a thread of blue(?) (antarant-) wool in the same way [and] speaks: 'Whoever has been making him blue(?) — now, see, I am taking the [b]lue(?) … (UD-an, 'day'?) from his whole body, [and] I am giving [i]t back to his master.' She winds the woollen thread around the figures.

[Afterw]ards she makes a thread of white wool in the same way and speaks: '[Whoever] has been bewitching him, whoever has been ašarešk-ing him (perhaps 'making him white'?) — [now], see, from all his limbs […], [and] I am giving [it] [ba]ck to his master.' [She winds] the thread aro[und] [the figures].
[…] [she places green wool] […] … […] has been making (him) pale […] 'Let the man take them back for himself […]; let the woman take (them) for herself!'

Afterwards she places white wool and speaks: 'Th[is] [white wool]: just as grievous(?) enmity is reconciled(?), and (as) this (is) sorcery (and) impurity, so let this white wool purify (it)! Whether someone did evil to him be[fore the gods], or [someone] did evil to him before mankind, now let this white wool take it from al[l] his limbs and give it to the sorcerous person. Let this person be pure before (them)!'

She throws all this onto the figures. The Old Woman picks up five loaves, one jug of beer (and) pegs of karšani-(wood?). She goes outside and digs (into) the earth nearby(?). She puts the implements of the ritual into it, heaps mud on top and levels it. She drives in the pegs and speaks as follows: 'Whoever has been bewitching this one — now I have taken back his sorcery, put it down into the earth and nailed it down. Let the sorceries (and) the evil dreams be nailed down, and let it not come up again! Let the Dark Earth hold it!'

She comes away from there a little, and beside the hole she breaks one flat bread for Marwaya(?). (For those) of the dog-man who roam about in front(?) she breaks one flat bread …(miyanit) tongue(?). She breaks one flat bread for the Dark Earth; she breaks one flat bread for the Sun-god, and speaks: 'You, protect this!' She breaks one flat bread for the Sun-god, puts them down on the ground, pours out beer before all the flat breads, and speaks: 'This evil sorcery — you (pl.) keep it [na]iled down!'

She co[mes] back a little [and] br[eaks] [one] [flat] bread for Ariya, puts it on the right side of the road, pours out beer and s[peaks]: 'You, seize this evil and do not [let] it go back!' She breaks one flat bread for the ḫattarešna- (roadside pit?) of the road, [puts it] on the left side of the road, pours out beer and speaks: 'Gods of the [roa]d, you (pl.) guard the evil, and let it not come [ba]ck!'

She goes forward a little and [breaks] one flat bread for the Šalawana-(gods) of the gate. She sets it down, pours out beer and speaks: 'Up(?) […] you (pl.), keep speaking good (things)! But the evil ones […] … GA[LA](?) […]' She breaks one jug apart, and […] it […].

She places kar(a)š-wheat, grain, paššu-breads, a [bow] (and) [three arrows] into a basket and [puts] it be[neath] the bed, and he (the patient) sleeps over it. And on the bed [she …] ešara-wool […], and she binds (it) at the RAPŠU (hip?).

On the second day, when it grows light, she takes the basket away from be[neath] the bed and swings it away over the person, and speaks: 'Dog-man, [you give] these sorceries b[ack] to the sorcerous person! And they (are) your …[…]' […] And she speaks: 'Let these [lift(?)] from him […]; let these [lift] from him from here […]; let them lift! But these from him from [the bed(?)] […]'

When it grows light, she takes the figures away [from beneath] the bo[wl] […], cuts off the linen thread and pla[ces] it on the figures. She [takes] for herself a clod of earth of the LAM.ḪAL-tree(?), keeps pressing [it] on him, and spea[ks]: 'Just as this earth purifies downwards(?), so [let it purify] this person, all (his) limbs, in the same way. And for him let it li[kewise] purify his house, al[tar] (and) hearth, together with [his] wife, her husband (and) his children!'

Afterwards she takes a l[ump](?) of dough, keeps pressing it on him [...] and spea[ks]: '[…] as […] keeps (something) alive, [so] this [person …], let (his) limbs likewise live! […] let [them] l[ikewise] [live]!'

She se[ts] the person down facing the Sun-god […] and h[olds] out the wax figures, and speaks: 'Whoever, whoev[er] (made) [sorc]ery […] — now they have done it, and s[e]e, … in front(?) […].' Thus (says) the human being: 'We are tired!' Thus (say) the fi[gures]: 'You (pl.) brought (it); we will carry (it) off(?).' 'But in return let the dog-man clothe (himself in them?) against him, and let him [put] them on (as shoes?) for you(?); let him protect him, and … them away […]'
'With a rake let him [ra]ke it away behind (him); with a [sho]vel let him [shove it] away behind (him)!' […] …uttar […] […]

[…] she finishes(?) and […] water […] pours, and therein into a clay cup […] [tariyattar]iya-(plant?); one clay cup of wardulli-(plant?); [one] [clay] cup of wine (with) a fresh vine-shoot (maḫla-); one clay cup […] … and they divide each one apart […] poured, and in each one […] lies. And the human being […] they bathe with NISABA (grain?).

[…] his [he]ad … tari[yattariya-] […] [and] [spea]ks […] [gap] … speaks […] and he […] one man … […] and speaks: '… […]' the kuptar- (?) in … […] [end of column III; gap] […] they … […] then the ear, [the liver] […] [and] they cook [them] on an open flame […] she places [the flat bread]s on top and speaks: '[…] … Sun-god …[…]' […] they cook (them) on an open flame and eat them up.

[And] [whe]n they have finished working the wax figures, she takes [the imple]ments: one sheep, five flat breads, groats (and) a jug of beer. [She] goes down to the river and lies down (there) for the night. On the bank of the river she (breaks) one flat bread for the Mother-goddess of the riverbank; into the river she breaks two flat breads for the welluwila- (meadow-spirits?) of the river, [sets them] down and pours out beer. Then she offers one sheep to these gods, and it … (text unclear). Then they take the meat: the liver, [the heart] (and) the short ribs, and they cook them on an open flame. She cuts [them] up and places them on the flat breads.

[The Old Woman] speaks: she speaks the name of the Mother-goddess of the riverbank (and) of the river: 'O […]s of the river, you (pl.) keep eating and keep drinking! To this […] keep giving … water!' And for him [the waters](?) inside […]. She pours a [cu]p of wine into the river. One sheep, the Old Wom[an] … they [tu]rn(?). They draw (water with) two [wine] cu[ps], and it came into the t[own](?). […] they pour (it) out towards the water, and he bathes (himself).

[Colophon:] One tablet, complete. [List of ritual materials:] […] …-lliš(?), on the third day …[…]; [a] kureššar-cloth, six wool[len] thr[eads](?) […]; [one] bow, three arrows, three naktamu-vessels […]; […] [of wa]x, one kurtal-box, one basket(?) …[…]; […] … one handful, two handfuls of groats […]; […] [tar]iyattariya- of the vine(?) […]; […] wardulli- (and) ašḫaul- […]; […] one sheep, one white lamb, four jugs of beer […].
